facts.statement: The only known species, Brachauchenius lucasi, was first described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1903 based on fossils found in Kansas.
facts.quote: Only one species is known, B. lucasi, initially described by Samuel Wendell Williston in 1903 from a partial fossil skeleton discovered in a quarry in Kansas, United States.

facts.statement: Additional specimens were found later, including one from Morocco that was officially assigned to the species in 2016.
facts.quote: Many other fossil specimens attributed to the species were subsequently discovered, including an individual from Morocco whose presence was made official in 2016.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton was discovered in 1884 by a quarry owner near Delphos, Ottawa County, Kansas.
facts.quote: In 1884, a partial skeleton of a marine reptile was discovered by the owner of a quarry near Delphos, in Ottawa County, Kansas.

facts.statement: Samuel Wendell Williston formally named the fossil Brachauchenius lucasi in 1903.
facts.quote: In 1903, Samuel Wendell Williston designated the fossil as the holotype of a new plesiosaur genus and species under the name Brachauchenius lucasi.

facts.statement: The genus name Brachauchenius means "short neck" in Ancient Greek and Latin.
facts.quote: The generic name Brachauchenius derives from the Ancient Greek words βραχύς (brakhys, "short") and αὐχήν (aukhḗn, "neck"), followed by the Latin suffix ius, all meaning "short neck".

facts.statement: Williston named the animal "short neck" because the holotype was believed to have the shortest neck of any described plesiosaur.
facts.quote: Williston chose this name because this specimen was considered the shortest-necked plesiosaur ever described.

facts.statement: Microscopic analysis in 2005 dated the holotype to the early Middle Turonian based on its origin in the Greenhorn Limestone or Fairport Chalk.
facts.quote: A microscopic examination of the fossils published in 2005 revealed that the specimen came from either the upper level of the Greenhorn Limestone or the lower level of the Fairport Chalk Member of the Carlile Shale, suggesting that the specimen dates to the early Middle Turonian.

facts.statement: Brachauchenius lived during the Late Cretaceous in regions that are now North America and North Africa.
facts.quote: Brachauchenius (meaning 'short neck') is an extinct genus of pliosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous in what are now North America and North Africa.

facts.statement: Brachauchenius had a large, elongated skull and a short neck, a morphology typical of thalassophonean pliosaurids.
facts.quote: Brachauchenius has a morphology typical of the pliosaurids of the thalassophonean group, which has a large elongated skull connected to a short neck, unlike many other plesiosaurs, which have a long neck and a small head.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Brachauchenius is estimated to have reached a maximum length of 5.3 meters and a body mass of 2.2 tons.
facts.quote: the holotype specimen having a maximum length estimated at 5.3 m for a body mass estimated at 2.2 t.

facts.statement: A relatively complete pliosaurid skeleton was discovered in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, in 2000 and exhumed between 2004 and 2005.
facts.quote: In 2000, a relatively complete pliosaurid skeleton, since cataloged as VL17052004-1, was discovered in the town of Villa de Leyva in Boyacá, Colombia, before being exhumed during 2004-2005.

facts.statement: A skeleton initially described as Brachauchenius in 2005 was reclassified as the new genus Stenorhynchosaurus munozi in 2016.
facts.quote: The skeleton was first described in 2005 by Oliver Hampe as belonging to Brachauchenius, before being designated as the holotype of a new genus and species under the name Stenorhynchosaurus munozi by María Eurídice Páramo and colleagues in 2016.

facts.statement: The skeleton of Stenorhynchosaurus munozi dates to the Upper Barremian, representing the oldest known example of the brachauchenines.
facts.quote: Coming from the Paja Formation, it was dated to the Upper Barremian, making the latter the oldest known example of the brachauchenines.

facts.statement: The holotype of Megacephalosaurus eulerti was discovered in 1950 by brothers Frank and Robert Jennrich near Fairport, Kansas.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of the genus, cataloged as FHSM VP-321, was discovered in 1950 by teenage brothers Frank and Robert Jennrich near Fairport, Kansas.

facts.statement: The Fairport skull was officially described as the new genus Megacephalosaurus eulerti in 2013 by Schumacher, Carpenter, and Everhart.
facts.quote: The specimen is then removed from its mount, and is officially described in 2013 by Bruce A. Schumacher, Carpenter and Everhart as the holotype of a new genus and species which they name Megacephalosaurus eulerti.

facts.statement: Photos found in 2007 revealed that the Fairport skull had underside features distinct from other Brachauchenius lucasi skulls.
facts.quote: In 2007, Everhart discovered photos of the skull's underside taken prior to its mounting, which revealed underside features that were different from those found in other B. lucasi skulls.

facts.statement: A skeleton from the Paja Formation in Colombia was initially thought to be Brachauchenius but was later moved to a new genus.
facts.quote: In 2000, a relatively complete pliosaurid skeleton, since cataloged as VL17052004-1, was discovered in the town of Villa de Leyva in Boyacá, Colombia, before being exhumed during 2004-2005.

facts.statement: It is debated whether some specimens currently attributed to Brachauchenius actually belong to the genus Megacephalosaurus.
facts.quote: Everhart blogged that other specimens currently attributed to Brachauchenius may actually belong to Megacephalosaurus.

facts.statement: Brachauchenius belongs to the family Pliosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Pliosauridae

facts.statement: The genus is classified within the subfamily Brachaucheninae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Brachaucheninae

facts.statement: The first known specimen, USNM 4989, was collected by Charles H. Sternberg in Ottawa County, Kansas, in 1884.
facts.quote: El primer espécimen conocido (holotipo), USNM 4989 fue recolectado por Charles H. Sternberg en el condado Ottawa, Kansas en 1884.

facts.statement: The species was named by S.W. Williston.
facts.quote: Esta especie fue nombrada por S.W. Williston

facts.statement: A larger specimen, FHSM VP-321, with a cranial length of 170 centimeters, was excavated by George F. Sternberg in 1952 from the Fairport Limestone in Russell County, Kansas, and later described by Carpenter.
facts.quote: Un espécimen mayor (FHSM VP-321 - longitud craneal de 170 centímetros) fue excavado por George F. Sternberg en 1952 en la caliza Fairport del condado Russell, Kansas, y más tarde descrito por Carpenter.

facts.statement: The type species, Brachauchenius lucasi, lived in the western interior sea of North America between 93.5 and 89.3 million years ago during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: La especie tipo, Brachauchenius lucasi, vivió en el mar interior occidental de Norteamérica hace cerca de 93.5-89.3 millones de años, durante el Turoniense en el Cretácico Superior.

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Barremian to the Turonian, spanning from 125.77 to 89.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Turonian (125.77 to 89.8 million years ago)

facts.statement: Brachauchenius represents the last appearance of a pliosaur in North America.
facts.quote: Brachauchenius representa la última aparición de un pliosaurio en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Brachauchenius means "short neck" and is an extinct genus of pliosaurs.
facts.quote: Brachauchenius (significa "cuello corto") es un género extinto de pliosaurios

facts.statement: This pliosaur grew to a body length of nearly 10 meters.
facts.quote: Este pliosaurio crecía hasta cerca de 10 metros de longitud corporal.

facts.statement: Later analyses showed that a Colombian specimen referred to Brachauchenius was distinct enough to warrant a new genus and species, named Stenorhynchosaurus munozi.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, los análisis posteriores de este espécimen colombiano mostraron que era lo suficientemente diferente como para merecer un nuevo género y especie, nombrado como Stenorhynchosaurus munozi.

facts.statement: The specimen FHSM VP-321 was later assigned to its own genus and species, Megacephalosaurus eulerti.
facts.quote: El espécimen FHSM VP-321 fue más tarde asignado a su propio género y especie, Megacephalosaurus eulerti.
